lines.text: A people who rode in from the east and built a kingdom on the Danube, then survived empires and occupations. This is the story of Hungary.
Around 895, the Magyars crossed the mountains and settled in the wide basin of the Danube, the land that would become Hungary.
Their prince Stephen was crowned king in the year 1000, and he made his people Christian.
With his crown, the kingdom of Hungary was born, a country of the middle Danube that endures to this day.
In the thirteenth century, kings built a royal castle on the hill above the Danube at Buda.
In the fifteenth century, King Matthias Corvinus made Buda a Renaissance court, with a great library and a strong army.
Then, in 1526 at Mohacs, the Ottomans crushed the Hungarian army, and the king was killed. For a century and a half, they held the centre.
Under the Habsburgs that followed, a new voice arose. Lajos Kossuth, born in 1802, would become Hungary's national hero.
Franz Liszt, born in 1811, became the most dazzling pianist in Europe, and invented the symphonic poem.
In 1848, led by Kossuth, Hungary rose against Habsburg rule. It took Russian troops to crush the revolution.
In 1849 the Chain Bridge opened, the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary, joining Buda and Pest.
In 1867 a compromise made Austria and Hungary two halves of one monarchy, and Hungary got a government of its own.
Six years later Buda, Obuda and Pest joined into one capital, Budapest, and the city boomed.
Bela Bartok, born in 1881, travelled the villages gathering folk songs, and turned them into modern music.
In 1904 the great Parliament on the Danube was finished, a symbol of the nation's pride.
But defeat in the First World War cost dearly. In 1920 the Treaty of Trianon took away two thirds of Hungary's land.
Ferenc Puskas, born in 1927, would star in the Golden Team of the fifties, and later for Real Madrid.
In 1944 about four hundred and forty thousand Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz. Most of them were murdered.
That same year, in Budapest, Erno Rubik was born, the architect whose puzzle would one day be known all over the world.
That winter, Soviet forces besieged Budapest, one of the bloodiest sieges of the war.
Katalin Kariko, born in 1955, would do the work on messenger RNA that made the COVID vaccines possible, and win a Nobel Prize.
In 1956, under a Soviet-backed government, students in Budapest began a revolt that spread across the country. Soviet tanks crushed it within weeks.
Viktor Orban, born in 1963, would become prime minister, and later hold power for sixteen years.
In 1974 Erno Rubik invented a puzzle cube of coloured faces. It became one of the best-selling toys of all time.
Peter Magyar, a lawyer born in 1981, would one day lead the Tisza party.
In 1989 a border gate opened for a picnic, and hundreds of East Germans fled west. The Iron Curtain was cracking.
And in April 2026, Peter Magyar's Tisza party won the election, ending Viktor Orban's sixteen years in power.
From the Magyar riders to a new government on the Danube, Hungary's story goes on.
